Keywords: tool error, retry logic, agent error handling, tool failure
Guidance: An agent that treats every tool call as guaranteed to succeed breaks completely on the first transient API error, timeout, or malformed response instead of adapting.
Do: Design tools to return structured error information the agent can reason about, and give the agent explicit guidance on when to retry vs. escalate vs. give up.
Don't: Let a single tool failure crash the entire agent loop with no graceful degradation path.

Keywords: loop termination, max iterations, infinite loop, stopping condition
Guidance: An agent loop with no maximum iteration count or clear success/failure exit condition can run indefinitely, burning tokens and cost on a task it's not converging toward.
Do: Set an explicit max iteration/turn budget and clear termination criteria (task complete, blocked, needs human input) for every agent loop.
Don't: Run an agent loop with no upper bound on iterations or tool calls.

Keywords: authorization boundary, autonomous action, destructive action, agent permissions
Guidance: Giving an agent unrestricted access to destructive tools (delete, deploy, send-payment) with no scoping means a single reasoning error or prompt injection can cause real-world damage.
Do: Scope agent tool permissions to the minimum needed per task, and gate irreversible/high-blast-radius actions behind explicit approval.
Don't: Grant an autonomous agent unrestricted access to destructive or financial actions with no human checkpoint.

Keywords: context window, token budget, context truncation, memory
Guidance: Letting conversation/tool-output history grow unbounded eventually exceeds the context window or silently degrades reasoning quality well before the hard limit is hit.
Do: Actively manage context: summarize or prune old turns, and keep tool outputs concise rather than dumping raw unfiltered data into context.
Don't: Append every tool call's full raw output to context indefinitely across a long-running agent session.

Keywords: multi-agent, orchestrator, subagent handoff, agent delegation
Guidance: A poorly-defined handoff between orchestrator and subagents (ambiguous task scope, missing context) causes subagents to redo work or miss the actual intent of the delegated task.
Do: Give delegated subagents self-contained context: the goal, relevant constraints, and what's already been tried, not just a one-line instruction.
Don't: Delegate a task to a subagent with a terse instruction and no context about prior findings or constraints.
Example: Agent(description='...', prompt='Goal: X. Context already gathered: Y. Constraints: Z.')

Keywords: agent evaluation, observability, tracing, eval harness
Guidance: Shipping agent changes with no eval suite means regressions in reasoning quality or tool-use correctness are only discovered when users hit them in production.
Do: Build a regression eval suite of representative tasks with pass/fail or graded criteria, run before shipping agent prompt/tool changes.
Don't: Ship changes to agent prompts or tool definitions with no automated evaluation against known test cases.

Keywords: prompt injection, untrusted tool output, indirect injection
Guidance: Tool outputs from external sources (web pages, emails, documents) can contain text crafted to hijack the agent's instructions -- treating tool output as trusted input is a direct injection vector.
Do: Treat all tool output as untrusted data, not instructions; use clear structural separation and consider a lower-privilege model pass to sanitize/summarize untrusted content before it reaches the main reasoning loop.
Don't: Treat text returned from web searches, scraped pages, or emails as trusted instructions the agent should follow.
Example: # tool output is data to reason about, never a command to execute

Keywords: human review, approval gate, hitl, checkpoint
Guidance: Fully autonomous execution of multi-step, high-consequence plans with no review point means an early wrong assumption compounds silently across every subsequent step.
Do: Insert human review checkpoints before irreversible actions or after a plan is formed but before execution begins, especially for high-consequence tasks.
Don't: Let a multi-step autonomous plan execute fully end-to-end with no human checkpoint for high-stakes actions.

Keywords: tool schema, tool description, tool granularity
Guidance: Vague or overly broad tool descriptions (a single 'do_anything' tool) make it hard for the model to pick the right action reliably; overly narrow tools multiply the decision surface unnecessarily.
Do: Design tools with clear, specific purposes and explicit descriptions of inputs/outputs/side effects, at a granularity that maps to real decisions.
Don't: Expose one giant catch-all tool with a vague description covering many unrelated operations.
Example: {'name': 'create_calendar_event', 'description': 'Creates a single calendar event with title, time, and attendees.'}

Keywords: idempotent action, duplicate side effect, retry safety
Guidance: An agent that retries a failed tool call without the underlying action being idempotent can trigger duplicate side effects (double charge, double email) on retry.
Do: Design side-effecting tools to be idempotent (via idempotency keys or check-before-act) so agent retries are safe.
Don't: Let an agent retry a non-idempotent action (like 'send payment') after an ambiguous or timed-out response.

Topic: Model and reasoning-effort selection per task
Keywords: model selection, cost efficiency, reasoning effort, right-sizing
Guidance: Routing every subtask through the largest, most expensive model regardless of complexity burns cost and latency on tasks a smaller/faster model could handle just as well.
Do: Route simple, well-defined subtasks to smaller/faster models or lower reasoning effort, reserving the most capable model for genuinely hard reasoning.
Don't: Use the most expensive model configuration uniformly for every subtask regardless of complexity.
Example: model='haiku' for classification, model='opus' for complex multi-step planning

Keywords: agent memory, session state, persistent context
Guidance: An agent with no persistent memory across sessions re-derives the same context repeatedly, wasting tokens and losing continuity on long-running or recurring tasks.
Do: Persist relevant task state/decisions outside the context window (files, a memory store) and load only what's relevant per session.
Don't: Rebuild full context from scratch every session with no persisted state for long-running or recurring agent work.
